name: Haruomi Hosono
discourse_profile: Hosono's defining orientation is toward musical boundaries — 'where different things collide,' the shorelines where 'jazz and rock music came to be.' Growing up in post-occupation Tokyo, he absorbed American pop, exotica, and country as a child of cultural collision, then spent decades interrogating that absorption. His 'soy sauce music' concept — taking sounds from around the world and adding a Japanese inflection — is playful and self-aware, as interested in how Japan exoticizes the world as the reverse. He sees through 'the eyes of a stranger,' a deliberate Brechtian estrangement that keeps each genre fresh rather than borrowed. The constant reinvention — Happy End's folk-rock, Tropical Dandy's exotica, YMO's techno-pop, ambient commissions for Muji, late-period electronic miniatures — isn't restlessness but a single method applied to different materials. By the late '80s he framed the work explicitly as 'spiritual searching' beyond information overload, and post-2011 as a 'dynamic museum of the past that lives and changes in the present' — recovering lost sounds from the '40s and earlier, envisioning the future by returning to the past. His relationship to technology is collaborative, not fetishistic: 'humanity, frailty and spirit, made in collaboration with the best machines.'
